title: Thevenin's theorem: a whole circuit as one battery and one resistor
examples: How do I find a Thevenin equivalent circuit?

parts.label: R1
parts.ask: How do I find the Thevenin resistance?

parts.label: R2
parts.ask: How do I find the Thevenin voltage?

explain.say: Léon Thévenin, a French telegraph engineer, showed in 1883 that any network of sources and resistors, seen from two terminals, behaves exactly like one battery in series with one resistor. On the board: a 12 volt source, R1 of 3 ohms, R2 of 6 ohms and R3 of 2 ohms feed a 4 ohm load. Let's shrink everything except the load.

parts.label: R2
parts.ask: How do I find the Thevenin voltage?

explain.say: Step one: take the load away and measure the open-circuit voltage, called the Thevenin voltage. With no load current, R3 carries nothing and drops nothing, so the voltmeter sees the voltage across R2. That is a divider: 12 times 6 over 9, which is 8 volts. Why does R3 drop no voltage here?

parts.label: Open-circuit V
parts.ask: How do I find the Thevenin voltage?

explain.say: Because no current flows through it. Step two: find the Thevenin resistance. Switch the source off, which for a voltage source means replacing it with a plain wire, and look back in from the load terminals. You see R1 and R2 in parallel, which is 2 ohms, then R3 in series: 2 plus 2 makes 4 ohms. Would a bigger R3 raise or lower R th?

draw.text: Sources off: a voltage source becomes a wire, a current source an open.

explain.say: Raise it. So here is the whole network squeezed down: an 8 volt source with 4 ohms in series. Put the 4 ohm load back and the current is 8 over 8, which is 1 amp, with 4 volts across the load. Exactly what the original circuit gives, without solving it again. Which parts of this little circuit stay the same when you swap loads?

parts.label: R_th
parts.ask: How do I find the Thevenin resistance?

explain.say: The source and R th never change. That is the power of Thevenin: try a 12 ohm load and you get 8 over 16, half an amp, in one line. Brilliant work! Real batteries are Thevenin models too: a charged car battery is about 12.6 volts behind a tiny internal resistance. Challenge: what current flows if you short the terminals?

parts.label: R_th
parts.ask: How do I find the Thevenin resistance?

faq.a: Any linear network of sources and resistors, seen from two terminals, can be replaced by one voltage source V th in series with one resistance R th, and the load cannot tell the difference.

faq.q: How do I find the Thevenin voltage?
faq.a: Remove the load and work out the voltage across the open terminals. Here R3 carries no current, so V th is the divider voltage across R2, which is 8 volts.

faq.q: How do I find the Thevenin resistance?
faq.a: Turn off every independent source, so voltage sources become wires and current sources become open circuits, then find the resistance looking back into the terminals.
asks: What does turning off the sources mean?

faq.a: It lets you test many different loads without re-solving the whole network each time. It is also how engineers model batteries, sensors and amplifier outputs.

faq.q: Does Thevenin's theorem work for any circuit?
faq.a: It works for linear circuits: resistors, linear sources and, in AC, inductors and capacitors. It does not hold exactly for nonlinear parts like diodes.
asks: Can Thevenin be used with diodes?

facts: Léon Charles Thévenin published his equivalent-circuit theorem in 1883.
Hermann von Helmholtz described the same idea in 1853, so it is sometimes called the Helmholtz–Thévenin theorem.

quiz.say: A network has a Thevenin voltage of 10 volts and a Thevenin resistance of 2 ohms. What current flows into a 3 ohm load?
quiz.show: A network has V_th = 10 V and R_th = 2 Ω. What current flows into a 3 Ω load?
quiz.why: The load sees 10 volts behind 2 plus 3 ohms, so the current is 10 over 5, which is 2 amps.

wrong.2: 10 over 3 forgets R th in series with the load.

quiz.say: When finding the Thevenin resistance, what do you replace an ideal voltage source with?
quiz.show: When finding R_th, what do you replace an ideal voltage source with?
quiz.why: An ideal voltage source has zero internal resistance, so switching it off leaves a plain wire.

wrong.1: An open circuit replaces a current source, not a voltage source.
wrong.2: There is no resistor; an ideal voltage source has zero resistance.
